title: ANALYSIS | Why this round of Stellantis, Unifor contract talks are 'unprecedented' | CBC News

Windsor·Analysis

'Unprecedented': Why this round of Stellantis, Unifor contract talks is like no other

'I've never been through a contract negotiation like this,' one Windsor, Ont., autoworker says

Back in the spring, Unifor Local 444 president James Stewart warned that this year's contract talks with global carmaker Stellantis would be the toughest round of bargaining ever in the powerful union's long history — even worse than during the 2008 financial crisis.

"I think any other round of negotiations is easy compared to what we're facing now," the Canadian union leader said in late May. "I think this is a much worse position for longevity and making sure we're around long term."

So far, Stewart seems to have been right.

The September deadline for the union's contract passed eight weeks ago without much fanfare.

The more than 6,000 workers Stewart represents at the Stellantis assembly plant in Windsor, Ont., have been repeatedly laid off, as have parts suppliers, with the automaker citing tariffs and lower consumer demand. Contract talks were stalled over Stellantis's plan to sell its plant in Brampton to a defence contractor.

The idled Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant in Ontario is seen on Aug. 19. (REUTERS/Carlos Osorio)

On top of all that, the provincial and federal governments are now involved, trying to make sure that plant has a future building cars — a future they say would help fuel the economy by keeping thousands of people there employed, in addition to the vast supply chain that supports the facility.

"I've been here 30 years — I've never been through a contract negotiation like this," Jeff Edward, an autoworker at the Windsor plant, said recently.

The path forward, for now, seems unclear, with the future of Stellantis's roughly 10,000 employees in Canada — and maybe the future of the industry itself — hanging in the balance.

  • Stellantis would owe feds $831M if sale of Brampton, Ont., plant proceeds: source

  • Video

    Stellantis workers back on the job after 4 weeks, shadow of Brampton plant sale

"This is unique and I would use the word anomalous, like it's an anomaly, and not so much that the union is doing something that's anomalous," said Herman Rosenfeld, a retired Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) staffer who worked in the education department for over a dozen years.

"They're facing a situation which is, if you look at the industry itself in Canada, it's in trouble in lots of ways."

'Unusual' that 'multiple players' involved in talks

Rosenfeld and others identify a common undercurrent today: A man in Washington with an oft-criticized and increasingly unpopular plan to revive American manufacturing by punishing a longtime trade partner he claims has taken advantage of the U.S.

"We don't want this Stellantis plant to be the first plant to close as a result of the disruption created by Donald Trump," says Ken Lewenza, who led the CAW for years before it merged with the Communications, Energy and Paperworkers Union of Canada to form Unifor in 2013.

Ken Lewenza, former president of the Canadian Auto Workers, is shown at his home in Windsor on Nov. 17. 'We don't want this Stellantis plant to be the first plant to close as a result of the disruption created by Donald Trump,' he says. (Emma Loop/CBC)

Lewenza said the current negotiations are "unprecedented," in large part because they involve an existential battle, rather than the typical fight over benefits and wages.

"The reality is there's multiple players involved in these negotiations, which by itself is unusual," he said. "But what we're trying to do is preserve as many jobs as we can in Canada. We're actually trying to preserve the manufacturing footprint of auto plants in Canada [that are] manufacturing vehicles."

Stellantis has cited the trade war as a key driver in its decision to sell Brampton. Another element to consider is the North American industry's retreat from electric vehicles (EVs) that has been fuelled in part by Trump's rollback of green energy initiatives.

A Stellantis employee works on an internal combustion engine at the company's assembly plant in Windsor on May 28. (Ken Amlin/CBC)

Before Stellantis halted retooling on the plant last year, the plan was for the Brampton plant — like the one in Windsor — to be upgraded to support both electric and gas-powered vehicle production.

Stellantis has received at least $220 million in federal funding for the upgrades to its Ontario facilities, as CBC Windsor first reported last year. The automaker has offered to repay $24 million it says it received for Brampton specifically. But Ottawa has said the company breached the funding agreement by closing and seeking to sell the plant, and is on the hook for "hundreds of millions."

  • Feds, Ontario offering Stellantis 'aggressive package' to keep Brampton auto plant open

  • Analysis

    Did Stellantis violate its deals with the feds? Funding contract provided exceptions around Brampton

Stewart and Unifor did not respond to interview requests for this story. But in a public update Wednesday night, the union said Stellantis has presented its first closure agreement for the Brampton members. The union also reiterated its opposition to the sale, though it continues to say it wants to try to avoid a strike.

Stellantis, in a statement to CBC Windsor, said it is "engaged in discussions with Unifor."

Workers at the Windsor Stellantis plant, shown on May 28, continue to work under the terms of the previous collective agreement until a new pact is in place. (Ken Amlin/CBC)

Beyond Brampton, the union has said it needs firmer production allotments to secure employment in Windsor and at the company's casting plant in Etobicoke in suburban Toronto.

For now, members at those facilities continue to work under the terms of the previous collective agreement. Stellantis said that contract "continues until the union ratifies a new agreement."

Premier, union head urge Ottawa to take action

On Friday, Stellantis's global CEO Antonio Filosa spoke with federal, provincial and union representatives to discuss the Brampton situation.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said after the meeting that Stellantis, a multinational facing financial challenges, identified penalties for Canada's greenhouse gas emissions as a major cost to doing business — in addition to tariffs and zero-emissions vehicle rules in Quebec and British Columbia.

Stellantis also released a statement, saying, "The future of our Canadian operations and our employees remained the focus of today’s second meeting with representatives of the Canadian and Ontario governments and Unifor. We remain committed to continuing constructive discussions."

Ford is urging the federal government to take action, as is Unifor national president Lana Payne.

Payne said Stellantis was "unwavering" in its decision to sell the plant at the start of the discussion.

"And then we talked more about proposals and eventually getting ourselves to a different place, what has to be done here to change this outcome."

Filosa, Ford said, is sending his "right-hand man" to Ontario early next week, and that the parties will keep talking.
